purpose: Desktop and Server instance routing, replayed. Each case carries the op (without the schema wrapper) and the answer the kernel must give: the parsed answer, or {"error": "<the exact Err string>"} when the request itself is malformed. ds-web replays the same file through the vendored WASM, so no rule about which live runtime an operation belongs to, or whose reply may still be applied, can be true on one host and not another.
source: ds-web/docs/project-and-instance-isolation-contract.md (Desktop instances and CLI targeting; acceptance items 1 and 4), 2026-09-12, under the owner's rulings of the same day: CLI/MCP to Desktop or Server is one surface, and a saved CLI selection never flips a live map's project.

Every select or list case with more than one candidate is replayed in several permutations and must answer identically: order never decides.

cases.why: A current instance mints its own id at start and publishes it with its lane, build, start and profile; the id is taken as given and nothing is derived.
A descriptor written before instance identity carries only the four fields version 1 always had, and still has to be enumerable and nameable, so an identity is derived from what it does say.
A restart re-rolls the ephemeral port, so the successor derives a different identity: a dead descriptor's id can never be answered by the process that replaced it.
The same reason from the other side: a new process id derives a new instance, so a reused port cannot make a new runtime look like the old one.
Two installs may publish the same origin and pid at different times; the profile is part of the derivation so Stable and Canary are never one instance.
The host sends the pairing token to whatever this answers, so the address is normalised here, once; two spellings of one origin are therefore one instance, as the derived id shows.
Version 1 is the compatibility promise of this whole slice: fields are added, the version is not, and a file that claims another one is not read.

cases.why: `ds desktop list` with nothing running answers an empty list rather than refusing: there is no ambiguity to report and nothing went wrong.
The projection a client prints is decided here so no host has to judge which handshake fields are safe: never the token, the address or the account.
The order an operator reads is the same on every host and in every enumeration, so the row they name is the row they meant.
Listing is also how a caller finds out why an instance is not an option, so the compatible ones are named when a requirement is given.
Asked without an identity the answer says nothing about compatibility rather than guessing, and the member is present and null so the shape never moves.
The same host bug the selection refuses: a listing that showed one instance twice would invite an operator to target a duplicate.

cases.why: Switching a view's project is the event the whole generation exists for; everything captured before it belongs to a view that no longer exists.
An account change invalidates in-flight work for the same reason a project switch does, and by the same counter rather than a second mechanism.
Signing out is a context change too: a reply that arrives afterwards must not be written into the signed-out view.
A view's generation starts at one, so advancing from zero means the host never established the view it is claiming to change.
The ordinary case: nothing changed while the operation ran, so the result is applied to the view that asked for it.
Acceptance item 3, stated as one comparison: a delayed reply from before the switch is refused rather than written into the new view.
